title: How I structure a Next.js portfolio that passes real client checks
excerpt: A practical layout for a developer portfolio: case studies with constraints, honest screenshots, clear contact paths, and pages that help buyers decide without fluff.
metaDescription: Structure a Next.js developer portfolio for clients: case studies, products, privacy/terms, and content that shows real work instead of generic filler.
author: Ali Hamza
body:
## Why portfolios fail client checks

Clients rarely hire from a hero line alone. They scan for proof: what you shipped, what broke, what you would do differently, and how to reach you. A portfolio that is only animations and buzzwords fails that scan.

I keep this site focused on four jobs: show shipped work, explain how it was built, offer useful products, and make contact obvious.

## The page set that matters

1. **Home** - one clear offer, selected projects, and a path to contact.
2. **Projects** - case studies with problem, constraints, stack, and screenshots.
3. **Products** - paid packs with includes, price, and checkout.
4. **Blog** - fewer posts that teach something I actually use (deployments, scoping, tooling).
5. **Privacy / Terms** - required trust pages if you sell or run ads.

Thin affiliate-style posts and empty product pages hurt trust. I would rather publish one solid deployment guide than ten generic "side hustle" articles.

## Case study template I reuse

Every project page should answer:

- Who needed this and what was painful?
- What constraints existed (time, stack, privacy)?
- What did we ship in the first useful version?
- What tradeoffs did we accept?
- Where can someone see a sanitized UI?

If a page cannot answer those, it is not ready.

## Technical choices on this site

- **Next.js App Router** for routes, metadata, and server components.
- **Vercel** for previews and production.
- **JSON content** for products and many blog posts so edits are reviewable in git.
- **Strict CSP** with an allowlist so analytics and AdSense can load without opening the whole web.

## What I avoid

- Claiming earnings I did not measure.
- Publishing auto-generated posts that could belong to any site.
- Hiding contact behind a maze of CTAs.
- Shipping product pages with empty problem/solution sections.

## Checklist before you call it done

- [ ] Three or more project case studies with real constraints
- [ ] Contact email and form path work on mobile
- [ ] Privacy and Terms linked in the footer
- [ ] Products have problem, solution, and includes filled in
- [ ] Blog posts teach a specific workflow you use

If you want help shipping a client MVP with a clear scope first, use the contact page and tell me what you are building.
